nt: The pronoun **I** is stated twice here for emphasis. David is emphasizing his own condition or state in contrast to his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for me, I am]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disgrace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am disgusting to them]

Here the word that is translated **they see me** does not clearly indicate when the action of seeing occurs. It could mean “whenever they see me” or refer to a specific instance. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [whenever they see me]

The expression **shake their head** describes a symbolic action by which people showed contempt or mockery. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [they show that they despise me by shaking their heads]

x.ASV: Help me, O Jehovah my God; Oh save me according to thy lovingkindness:
x.Darby: Help me, Jehovah myGod; save me according to thy loving-kindness:
x.KJV: Help me, O Lord my God: O save me according to thy mercy:
x.YLT: Help me, O Jehovah my God, Save me, according to Thy kindness.

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please help me]

The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships as modeled in the UST. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to your covenant to be faithful]

By **according to your covenant faithfulness**, David means according to God’s promise to be faithful to his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [since you have promised to be faithful to me]

x.ASV: That they may know that this is thy hand; That thou, Jehovah, hast done it.
x.Darby: That they may know that this is thy hand; that thou, Jehovah, hast done it.
x.KJV: That they may know that this is thy hand; that thou, Lord, hast done it.
x.YLT: And they know that this is Thy hand, Thou, O Jehovah, Thou hast done it.

nt: Here, **so that** marks **they know that this is your hand; you, Yahweh, you have done it** as the goal or purpose of “Help me, Yahweh my God; save me according to your covenant faithfulness” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [because I want them to know]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [so that the people who accuse me know]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that this is your doing]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have done it** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who has acted. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [it is you, Yahweh, who have done it]

The pronoun **it** refers to Yahweh saving David, as he asked Yahweh to do in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh, are the one who saved me]

x.ASV: Let them curse, but bless thou: When they arise, they shall be put to shame, But thy servant shall rejoice.
x.Darby: Let them curse, but bless thou; when they rise up, let them be ashamed, and let thy servant rejoice.
x.KJV: Let them curse, but bless thou: when they arise, let them be ashamed; but let thy servant rejoice.
x.YLT: They revile, and Thou dost bless, They have risen, and are ashamed, And Thy servant doth rejoice.

nt: The pronoun **They** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people who accuse me, they will curse]

David is stating the pronouns **they** and **you** separately for emphasis, even though the verbs translated as **they will curse** and **you will bless** already include their meanings. He is doing that to create a strong contrast between what his enemies will do (curse) and what God will do (bless). If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [They are the ones who will curse, but you are the one who will bless]

By **they arise**, David means they arise to attack him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they arise to attack me]

The psalmist is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [and I, your servant]

x.ASV: Let mine adversaries be clothed with dishonor, And let them cover themselves with their own shame as with a robe.
x.Darby: Let mine adversaries be clothed with confusion, and let them cover themselves with their shame as with a mantle.
x.KJV: Let mine adversaries be clothed with shame, and let them cover themselves with their own confusion, as with a mantle.
x.YLT: Mine accusers put on blushing, and are covered, As an upper robe is their shame.

nt: יִלְבְּשׁ֣וּ שׂוֹטְנַ֣⁠י כְּלִמָּ֑ה וְ⁠יַעֲט֖וּ כַ⁠מְעִ֣יל בָּשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם

These two phrases **May my accusers be clothed with disgrace** and **may they wear their shame like a robe** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [May my accusers be clothed with shameful disgrace as though it were a robe]

Here David is speaking of his accusers as if they were people who could be **clothed with disgrace**. He means that their disgrace should be clearly seen and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May it be obvious how disgraceful my accusers are]

David is making a comparison between **their shame** and **a robe**. The point of this comparison is that just as a robe is visible to everyone who sees the person wearing it, so David wants his accusers’ shame to be visible and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [may their shame be so obvious to everyone that it is like a robe that they are wearing]

x.ASV: I will give great thanks unto Jehovah with my mouth; Yea, I will praise him among the multitude.
x.Darby: I will greatly celebrate Jehovah with my mouth; yea, I will praise him among the multitude.
x.KJV: I will greatly praise the Lord with my mouth; yea, I will praise him among the multitude.
x.YLT: I thank Jehovah greatly with my mouth, And in the midst of many I praise Him,

nt: Here, **mouth** represents speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak to greatly thank Yahweh]

David is using the adjective **many** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and in the midst of many people]

x.ASV: For he will stand at the right hand of the needy, To save him from them that judge his soul.
x.Darby: For he standeth at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those that judge his soul.
x.KJV: For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul.
x.YLT: For He standeth at the right hand of the needy, To save from those judging his soul.

nt: Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could physically **stand at the right hand of the needy**. The image of standing at someone’s right hand means to be ready to help and defend them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [he advocates for the needy] or [he helps the needy]

David is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

By **the judges of his soul**, David means those who seek to condemn him to death. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from officials who want to take his life]
